You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this — finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool — does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only — your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)

- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace

# Chroma - A General Purpose Syntax Highlighter

Chroma is a syntax highlighting library and command-line tool that takes source code and other structured text and converts it into syntax highlighted HTML, ANSI-coloured text, and other formats.

## Supported Languages

Chroma supports hundreds of programming languages and file formats, including:

## Try it

Try out various languages and styles on the [Chroma Playground](https://swapoff.org/chroma/playground/).

## Command-line Interface

A command-line interface to Chroma is included.

Binaries are available to install from [the releases page](https://github.com/alecthomas/chroma/releases).

### Usage with `less`

The CLI can be used as a preprocessor to colorise output of `less(1)`,
see documentation for the `LESSOPEN` environment variable.

The `--fail` flag can be used to suppress output and return with exit status
1 to facilitate falling back to some other preprocessor in case chroma
does not resolve a specific lexer to use for the given file. For example:

```shell
export LESSOPEN='| p() { chroma --fail "$1" || cat "$1"; }; p "%s"'
```

Replace `cat` with your favourite fallback preprocessor.

When invoked as `.lessfilter`, the `--fail` flag is automatically turned
on under the hood for easy integration with [lesspipe shipping with
Debian and derivatives](https://manpages.debian.org/lesspipe#USER_DEFINED_FILTERS);
for that setup the `chroma` executable can be just symlinked to `~/.lessfilter`.

## Projects using Chroma

* [`moor`](https://github.com/walles/moor) is a full-blown pager that colorizes
  its input using Chroma
* [Hugo](https://gohugo.io/) is a static site generator that [uses Chroma for syntax
  highlighting code examples](https://gohugo.io/content-management/syntax-highlighting/)

# Chroma - A General Purpose Syntax Highlighter

Chroma is a syntax highlighting library and command-line tool that takes source code and other structured text and converts it into syntax highlighted HTML, ANSI-coloured text, and other formats.

## Supported Languages

Chroma supports hundreds of programming languages and file formats, including:

| Prefix | Language
| :----: | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Try it

Try out various languages and styles on the [Chroma Playground](https://swapoff.org/chroma/playground/).

## Command-line Interface

A command-line interface to Chroma is included.

Binaries are available to install from [the releases page](https://github.com/alecthomas/chroma/releases).

### Usage with `less`

The CLI can be used as a preprocessor to colorise output of `less(1)`,
see documentation for the `LESSOPEN` environment variable.

The `--fail` flag can be used to suppress output and return with exit status
1 to facilitate falling back to some other preprocessor in case chroma
does not resolve a specific lexer to use for the given file. For example:

```shell
export LESSOPEN='| p() { chroma --fail "$1" || cat "$1"; }; p "%s"'
```

Replace `cat` with your favourite fallback preprocessor.

When invoked as `.lessfilter`, the `--fail` flag is automatically turned
on under the hood for easy integration with [lesspipe shipping with
Debian and derivatives](https://manpages.debian.org/lesspipe#USER_DEFINED_FILTERS);
for that setup the `chroma` executable can be just symlinked to `~/.lessfilter`.

## Projects using Chroma

* [`moor`](https://github.com/walles/moor) is a full-blown pager that colorizes
  its input using Chroma
* [Hugo](https://gohugo.io/) is a static site generator that [uses Chroma for syntax
  highlighting code examples](https://gohugo.io/content-management/syntax-highlighting/)

import subprocess

def run(args, stdin=None):
    r = subprocess.run(["./executable"]+args, input=stdin, capture_output=True)
    return r.returncode, r.stdout, r.stderr

# Try to brute force lexer XML format
# Common chroma lexer XML might be like:
# <lexer>
#   <config name="foo" aliases="foo" filenames="*.foo" mime-types="..."/>
#   <rules>
#     <state name="root">
#       <rule pattern="..."> <token type="..."/> </rule>
#     </state>
#   </rules>
# </lexer>
# Let's try variations and see if any change output from plaintext

candidates = [
    # Try 1: minimal with config + rules
    '''<lexer><config name="Test"/><rules><state name="root"><rule pattern="x"><token type="Keyword"/></rule></state></rules></lexer>''',
    '''<lexer><config name="Test" aliases="test"/><rules><state name="root"><rule pattern="x"><token type="Keyword"/></rule></state></rules></lexer>''',
    # Try 2: rule with type attribute?
    '''<lexer><config name="Test"/><rules><state name="root"><rule pattern="x" type="Keyword"/></state></rules></lexer>''',
    # Try 3: different casing?
    '''<lexer><config name="Test"/><rules><state name="root"><rule><pattern>x</pattern><token type="Keyword"/></rule></state></rules></lexer>''',
    # Try 4: Maybe root element is <lexers>?
    '''<lexers><lexer><config name="Test"/><rules><state name="root"><rule pattern="x"><token type="Keyword"/></rule></state></rules></lexer></lexers>''',
]

for i,c in enumerate(candidates):
    open("/tmp/l.xml","w").write(c)
    rc,out,err = run(["--lexer","/tmp/l.xml","--style","monokai","--formatter","tokens","--trace"], stdin=b'x=1\n')
    print(f"cand{i}: rc={rc} out={out!r} err={err!r}")

# Also test lexer file that is actually a style file? Should fallback?
# And test lexer with alias that matches builtin but file exists with same name? Precedence?
# If lexer value is "python" and file "python" exists in cwd, which wins? builtin or file?
open("./python","w").write('<style name="test"><entry type="Operator" style="#ff0000"/></style>')
rc,out,err = run(["--lexer","python","--style","monokai","--formatter","tokens"], stdin=b'x=1\n')
print(f"lexer python with file ./python present: {out!r} err={err!r}")
import os

print(f"lexer ./nonexistent: {out!r} err={err!r}")

# What about absolute path that doesn't exist?
rc,out,err = run(["--lexer","/tmp/doesnotexist12345.xml","--style","monokai","--formatter","tokens"], stdin=b'x=1\n')
print(f"lexer /tmp/doesnotexist: {out!r} err={err!r}")

import subprocess, os

def run(args, stdin=None, cwd=None):
    r = subprocess.run(["/workspace/executable"]+args, input=stdin, capture_output=True, cwd=cwd)
    return r.returncode, r.stdout, r.stderr

# So:
# - /tmp/testlexer.foo (EXISTS, unknown ext) -> error open ../tmp/testlexer.foo: invalid argument
# - /tmp/nonexistent.foo (NOT EXISTS, unknown ext) -> fallback plaintext, no error
# - foo.py (NOT EXISTS, known ext .py) -> Python lexer! So even non-existent file with known ext gives that lexer.
# - /tmp/a/b/c.py (NOT EXISTS, known ext) -> Python lexer

import subprocess, re

def run(args, stdin=None):
    r = subprocess.run(["./executable"]+args, input=stdin, capture_output=True)
    return r.returncode, r.stdout, r.stderr

# Compare html-styles vs full html CSS vs all-styles
rc,out_styles,_ = run(["--lexer","python","--style","monokai","--html","--html-styles"], stdin=b'x=1\n')
rc,out_full,_ = run(["--lexer","python","--style","monokai","--html"], stdin=b'x=1\n')

m=re.search(b'<style.*?</style>', out_full, re.DOTALL)
css_full = m.group(0) if m else b''
print(f"styles len {len(out_styles)}, full html len {len(out_full)}, css in full len {len(css_full)}")
# Compare styles vs css in full (strip <style> tags)
# styles is raw CSS, full's CSS is wrapped in <html>\n<style>...</style>
# Let's get full's CSS content
m2=re.search(b'<style type="text/css">\n(.*?)\n</style>', out_full, re.DOTALL)
css_content = m2.group(1) if m2 else b''
print(f"css_content len {len(css_content)}")
print(f"styles == css_content? {out_styles.strip() == css_content.strip()}")
# Show diff?
if out_styles.strip() != css_content.strip():
    # Find first diff
    a=out_styles.decode().split("\n")
    b=css_content.decode().split("\n")
    print(f"styles lines {len(a)}, full css lines {len(b)}")
    for i,(x,y) in enumerate(zip(a,b)):
        if x!=y:
            print(f"diff at {i}: styles:{x!r} vs full:{y!r}")

def format_terminal(tokens, style_dict, formatter):
    # formatter in terminal, terminal8, terminal16, terminal256, terminal16m
    out_chunks=[]
    for t,v in tokens:
        eff = get_effective_style(style_dict, t)
        prefix=""
        if eff.get("bold")==True:
            prefix+="\x1b[1m"
        if eff.get("underline")==True:
            prefix+="\x1b[4m"
        if eff.get("italic")==True:
            prefix+="\x1b[3m"
        fg_hex = eff.get("fg")

        if fg_hex:
            prefix+=hex_to_ansi_fg(fg_hex[1:], formatter)
        if bg_hex:
            prefix+=hex_to_ansi_bg(bg_hex[1:], formatter)
        has_style = (prefix!="")
        subparts=v.split("\n")
        for i, part in enumerate(subparts):
            if i>0:
                out_chunks.append("\n")
            if i==len(subparts)-1 and part=="" :
                # Last empty (after trailing \n or empty value): nothing
                continue
            if part=="":
                # Middle empty (blank line): if has_style, output prefix+reset, else nothing
                if has_style:
                    out_chunks.append(prefix+"\x1b[0m")
                # else nothing
            else:
                if has_style:
                    out_chunks.append(prefix+part+"\x1b[0m")

    fg = hex_to_ansi_fg(hex6, formatter)
    if not fg:
        return ""
    # Convert fg prefix to bg by replacing codes
    # For terminal: \x1b[33m -> \x1b[43m, \x1b[1m\x1b[31m -> \x1b[1m\x1b[41m (keep bold, replace 3X with 4X)
    # For terminal16: \x1b[33m -> \x1b[43m, \x1b[91m -> \x1b[101m (91->101, 90->100, etc.)
    # For 256: \x1b[38;5;NNNm -> \x1b[48;5;NNNm
    # For 16m: \x1b[38;2;R;G;Bm -> \x1b[48;2;R;G;Bm
    if formatter in ("terminal","terminal8"):
        # Replace \x1b[3Xm with \x1b[4Xm (X 0-7), keep \x1b[1m as is
        bg = fg.replace("\x1b[3", "\x1b[4")
        return bg
    elif formatter=="terminal16":
        # Replace 30-37 with 40-47, 90-97 with 100-107
        # fg is single code like \x1b[33m or \x1b[91m
        if "\x1b[3" in fg:
            return fg.replace("\x1b[3", "\x1b[4")
        elif "\x1b[9" in fg:
            # \x1b[91m -> \x1b[101m (9X -> 10X)
            # Extract digit after 9
            m=re.match(r"\x1b\[9(\d)m", fg)
            if m:
                d=m.group(1)
                return f"\x1b[10{d}m"
            return fg.replace("\x1b[9", "\x1b[10")
        return fg
    elif formatter=="terminal256":
        return fg.replace("\x1b[38;", "\x1b[48;")
    elif formatter=="terminal16m":
        return fg.replace("\x1b[38;", "\x1b[48;")
